tidbits.text: India's first patent was granted in 1856 — for an invention related to the process of making 'punkah pulling machines' (a type of ceiling fan)!
tidbits.verify: History of Indian Patent Office – ipindia.gov.in. The first Indian Patent Act (Act VI of 1856) was modelled on the British Patent Law of 1852.

tidbits.text: The Indian Patent Office has branches in Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and New Delhi. Any Indian citizen can file a patent application at any of these offices.
tidbits.verify: Indian Patent Office has four branches – ipindia.gov.in/patent-offices.htm

tidbits.text: In India you cannot patent a method of agriculture or horticulture. This ensures traditional farming practices remain freely available to all farmers.
tidbits.verify: Section 3(h) of the Patents Act, 1970 – Methods of agriculture or horticulture are not patentable.

tidbits.text: The oldest registered trademark still in use globally is the red triangle of Bass Brewery, registered in 1876. In India, the Trade Marks Registry was established in 1940 in Mumbai!
tidbits.verify: Trade Marks Registry history – ipindia.gov.in/trade-marks.htm. The Registry was established under the Trade Marks Act, 1940.

tidbits.text: A trademark can be a word, logo, sound, shape or even a colour combination! In India, the 'Yahoo!' yodel was one of the first sound marks to be discussed.
tidbits.verify: Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 defines a 'mark' to include a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging, or combination of colours.

tidbits.text: India has a special category of 'Well-Known Trademarks'. Brands like Tata, Reliance, and Amul are recognised as well-known marks, giving them extra protection across all goods and services.
tidbits.verify: Section 2(1)(zg) and Section 11(6)-(9) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 provide for well-known trademarks.

tidbits.text: In India, copyright protection is automatic — you get it the moment you create an original work! Registration is optional but helps as evidence in court.
tidbits.verify: The Copyright Act, 1957 does not mandate registration for copyright protection to exist. Section 45 provides for voluntary registration.

tidbits.text: The Indian Copyright Act protects 'folk songs' and 'folklore' under special provisions to preserve India's rich cultural heritage.
tidbits.verify: Section 31A of the Copyright Act, 1957 provides compulsory licences for certain works including works of cultural importance.

tidbits.text: Singing a copyrighted song at a school function for educational purposes is generally allowed under 'fair dealing' in India — but selling recordings of it is not!
tidbits.verify: Section 52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957 allows performance of a literary, dramatic, or musical work by staff and students of an educational institution in the course of activities of the institution.

tidbits.text: India is one of the world's largest producers of textiles, and many unique fabric patterns are registered as designs to protect the creativity of Indian weavers and artisans.
tidbits.verify: The Designs Act, 2000 protects the visual design of objects including textile designs. India has a rich tradition of GI-tagged and design-registered textiles.

tidbits.text: A design registration protects only how a product LOOKS, not how it WORKS. If you want to protect how it works, you need a patent instead!
tidbits.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 – Design means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to any article, judged solely by the eye.

tidbits.text: The Designs Act, 2000 replaced the older Designs Act of 1911. India modernised its design laws to keep up with global standards and to better protect creative industries.
tidbits.verify: The Designs Act, 2000 (Act 16 of 2000) came into force on 11 May 2001, replacing the Designs Act, 1911.
